design_detail: Anonymous online survey (Global Drug Survey, November-December 2011), promoted with Mixmag and The Guardian and on social media; 14,966 respondents, of whom 2513 had ever used synthetic cannabis and 980 had used it in the last 12 months. The 980 people who had used synthetic cannabis in the last year rated synthetic and natural cannabis on twelve effect domains (1-10) and on onset, time to peak and duration of effect when smoked; comparisons by dependent t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
can_establish: How a large self-selected sample of people who had recently used synthetic cannabis, almost all of whom also used natural cannabis, compared the two in retrospect, including after-effects such as hangover and ability to function after use.
cannot_establish: How synthetic cannabinoids actually affect people (no measurement, products of unknown content, recall and preference likely colour the ratings), how common these after-effects are in the general population, or how today's products compare (survey from 2011).

sample.recruitment: Self-nominating online sample through media partners and social networks; 15,200 responses, 52% from the UK and 23% from the USA; among people who had used synthetic cannabis in the last year 49% from the US and 27% from the UK (pp. 2-3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All respondents; the effect comparisons were asked of people who reported synthetic cannabis use in the last 12 months.
sample.demographics: People who had used synthetic cannabis in the last year: 79.6% male, median age 23 (interquartile range 19-28), 66.6% working and 53.3% studying, 90.8% White (p. 3).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; missing answers median 2% (range 0-14%) handled by available-case analysis (p. 2).
sample.selection_effects: Readers of a dance-music magazine and a newspaper, and their social networks; no sampling frame, no response rate; the authors call the sample self-nominating and poorly characterised (p. 5). Multiple entries could not be excluded (no IP addresses kept).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported use (lifetime, last year, days in the last month) of synthetic and natural cannabis; product names and contents unknown.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: smoked synthetic cannabis products; of the 356 who used in the last month, median 3 days of use (interquartile range 1-8), one third once only and 4.8% daily; 60.6% of those who had used in the last year had not used in the last 30 days; natural cannabis was used far more often (median 17 days in the last month among the 800 who used it in the last month) (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Very common: in the last month 90.5% drank alcohol, 88.4% used natural cannabis, 75.2% tobacco; in the last year about half used MDMA and about a third mushrooms, cocaine, LSD or benzodiazepines (Table 1, p. 3); not used to adjust the comparisons.

comparison.controls: Each respondent's own ratings of natural cannabis (within-person comparison).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; reasons for preferring either product were asked only of those preferring synthetic cannabis.

outcomes.instruments: Twelve self-rated effect domains (pleasurable effects when high, increase in appetite, sedation or sleepiness after use, value for money, ability to function after use, memory impairment, addictiveness, consistency of product, hangover effects, paranoia, harmful effects on lungs, negative effects when high), each rated for both products; onset, time to peak and duration of effect when smoked, in categories; overall preference (pp. 2-4).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation; the authors cite their earlier use of some items in a mephedrone survey (p. 2). Hangover effects are not defined in the paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Difference between each person's rating of synthetic and of natural cannabis.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; with about 850-930 respondents per comparison, every difference reached p<0.01.

analysis.effect_sizes: Dependent-samples t-tests with Cohen's d (Table 2, p. 5): hangover effects 3.49 (SD 2.80) against 2.79 (2.31), difference 0.70 (3.16), t(854) = 6.45, d = 0.22; ability to function after use 5.47 (2.76) against 6.85 (2.34), d = -0.45; sedation 4.51 against 6.16, d = -0.55; negative effects when high 4.80 against 2.80, d = 0.64; paranoia 4.75 against 3.89, d = 0.27; pleasurable effects 4.98 against 8.59, d = -1.22. Duration of peak effect: two thirds reported 1 h for synthetic cannabis, three quarters 2 h or more for natural cannabis (Wilcoxon z = -17.82); time to peak shorter for synthetic (z = -9.44); onset not different (z = 1.11, p = 0.268) (Fig. 2, p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Most comparisons are reported; the measures list a domain on the nature of sleep after use that appears in Table 2 as sedation (sleepiness after use).
analysis.power: Large sample; small differences reach significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Respondents rated synthetic cannabis as much less pleasurable, somewhat worse for functioning afterwards, with more negative effects while high, slightly more paranoia and slightly more hangover than natural cannabis, with a shorter high; 93% preferred natural cannabis.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say people who use both report a strong preference for natural cannabis and that synthetic cannabis has a less desirable effect profile (pp. 1, 4); this describes the ratings fairly. The Discussion's view that people who use both can differentiate the two (p. 4) and the conclusion's call to publicize the less desirable effect profile (p. 5) go beyond self-ratings by a self-selected group whose ratings may follow their preference; the Limitations acknowledge self-selection, unknown composition, polydrug use and recall bias (p. 5).

timeline.event: Vandrey et al. and Barratt et al., earlier online surveys of 168 and 316 people who used synthetic cannabinoids, cited in the introduction (most also used cannabis).
This survey, the largest of its kind at the time by the authors' account.

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive snapshot of how people who used both products compared them in 2011, when the synthetic cannabinoids on sale were different from later ones.

funding.funder: Global Drug Survey is self-funded; one author is funded by the National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University, itself funded by the Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing; the funders had no role in design, interpretation or write-up (p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: The first author is founder and managing director of Global Drug Survey; the second is on its expert advisory group (p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: South London and Maudsley NHS Trust and King's College London; Global Drug Survey; National Drug Research Institute, Curtin University.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective studies, or controlled studies where ethics allow, that measure next-day functioning and symptoms after identified synthetic cannabinoids against natural cannabis, with toxicology confirming what was used.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No sampling frame: readers of partner media and their social networks.
980 people who had used synthetic cannabis in the last year, about 850-930 per comparison.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics, countries, cannabis and other drug use described (pp. 2-3).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Missing data low (median 2%), but the sample's relation to all people who use synthetic cannabis is unknown.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Single unvalidated 1-10 items with no definition of hangover; product content unknown.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same online items for everyone, but retrospective ratings of two products at once invite anchoring and recall bias; the scale is given as 0-10 in Methods and 1-10 in Results.
Paired tests and effect sizes suit within-person ratings, but ordinal 1-10 items are analysed as interval data and there is no correction for multiple comparisons.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Open online survey without a denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of how a large, self-selected group of people who used both products compared them, the survey is informative and transparent about its limits. As evidence of what synthetic cannabinoids do the day after, it is weak: the ratings are retrospective, comparative and unvalidated, the products unknown and the sample self-selected. Cite it for the ratings in this sample only.

key_findings.finding: Of 14,966 respondents, 2513 (16.8%) had ever used synthetic cannabis and 980 (40.6% of 2417 answering) had used it in the last 12 months; 99.3% of these (of 975) had used natural cannabis, 95.0% in the last year.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 1st paragraph (p. 2, right column, continuing on p. 3); 3.3, 1st paragraph (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated effects (1-10), synthetic against natural cannabis, mean (SD): hangover effects 3.49 (2.80) against 2.79 (2.31), difference 0.70 (3.16), t(854) = 6.45, p<0.001, d = 0.22; ability to function after use 5.47 (2.76) against 6.85 (2.34), difference -1.38 (3.10), t(884) = -13.3, d = -0.45; sedation (sleepiness after use) 4.51 (2.57) against 6.16 (2.05), d = -0.55.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, hangover, ability to function and sedation rows
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered page; Table 2 prints d for ability to function with a doubled minus sign.

key_findings.finding: Also from Table 2: negative effects when high 4.80 (2.89) against 2.80 (2.00), d = 0.64; paranoia 4.75 (3.11) against 3.89 (2.43), d = 0.27; harmful effects on lungs 5.79 against 4.19, d = 0.56; pleasurable effects when high 4.98 (2.49) against 8.59 (1.70), d = -1.22; increase in appetite 3.79 against 6.89, d = -1.06; memory impairment 4.26 against 4.59, d = -0.12; addictiveness 2.62 against 2.97, d = -0.12.

When smoked, about 60% reported onset within 5 min for both products (z = 1.11, p = 0.268); over half reported the peak within 5 min for synthetic cannabis against 6-10 min most commonly for natural cannabis (z = -9.44, p<0.001); two thirds felt stoned for only 1 h after a typical smoke of synthetic cannabis, while three quarters felt natural cannabis for 2 h or longer (z = -17.82, p<0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.5, 1st paragraph (p. 4, left column, continuing to the right column); Fig. 2 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: 93% preferred natural cannabis; of the 69 (7.2% of 956) who preferred synthetic cannabis, the main reasons were its effect (58%), availability (19%), not being detected in urine tests (15%) and cost (9%).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Results 3.5, last paragraph (p. 4, right column)

key_findings.finding: Patterns: 60.6% of those who had used synthetic cannabis in the last year had not used it in the last 30 days; of the 356 who had, median 3 days of use, a third once only and 4.8% daily; 79.5% used natural cannabis on more days than synthetic cannabis.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the Wilcoxon statistic for the shorter duration of synthetic cannabis as z = 17.82, while Fig. 2C gives z = -17.82.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sign convention only; the direction (shorter for synthetic cannabis) is stated consistently in words.

reporting_issues.issue: The effect domains are said to be rated 0-10 in the Methods (p. 2) and 1-10 in the Results and Table 2 (pp. 4-5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the means cannot be compared exactly with other scales.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the effect size for ability to function after use as d = --0.45, with a doubled minus sign.
The Methods list a domain on the nature of sleep after use, which appears in Table 2 as sedation (sleepiness after use).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sleep item measures sleepiness, not sleep quality.
